title: A House for the Winter
premise: Elodie Joubert fled to the remote village of Sainte-Marthe to host a late-night radio show nobody listens to, hiding under a dead woman's identity with her two found-family strays, teen runaway Théo and mute old soldier Bram. Then her switchboard lights up with calls from villagers who died the previous week, and the church bell that was melted down in 1911 begins to ring each dusk. Sainte-Marthe has an old covenant: every winter the village must offer up a household, and the dead call the living home to be counted. When the count reaches her false name, Elodie must decide whether to keep running, surrender herself in place of the family she never meant to make, or break the covenant by giving the dead what they actually want: to be remembered. In the end she broadcasts the true names of every soul the village erased, the bell falls silent, and the family walks out ahead of the count—but Elodie stays behind as the village's new voice, half-claimed, speaking for the dead each winter so no one else is taken.
about_author: Kestrel Amberdale is the pen name of a former night-shift radio operator who spent years reading obituaries on air in rural France. Their work blends folk horror with quiet domestic tenderness, and they insist all their books are written between midnight and four.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. A routine night hosting the near-unlistened Sainte-Marthe community radio hour; we learn she lives under a borrowed identity with Théo and Bram. At 2 a.m. the switchboard lights up: a caller describes her own funeral from last week. Emotional beat: unease disguised as professional calm.

chapters.title: The Second Voice
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. She assumes a prank, but the caller knows details only the dead woman could know, including Elodie's real name—her true one, the one she buried. She checks the parish records; the woman died eight days ago. Beat: the first crack in her disbelief.

chapters.title: Household of Strays
chapters.summary: Théo's POV. Domestic morning at the rented farmhouse—burnt toast, Bram's silence, Théo's fear of being sent back. Elodie lies badly about being tired. Beat: warmth, and how much Elodie has to lose.

chapters.title: The Bell That Isn't
chapters.summary: Bram's POV, sparse and observational. At dusk a bell tolls; there is no bell—the 1911 record confirms it was melted for the war effort. Villagers pull their curtains shut. Beat: dread entering the village itself.

chapters.title: Calls from the Cold
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. More callers, all dead last week, all asking to be 'counted in.' The mayor, Madame Roux, warns her: don't answer the phone after the bell. Beat: Elodie's skepticism curdling into complicity—she keeps taking the calls anyway.

chapters.title: What Théo Heard
chapters.summary: Théo's POV. Théo answers the farmhouse phone by mistake and hears his dead mother's voice, gentle, asking him to come home. He doesn't tell Elodie. Beat: guilt, longing, the covenant finding his softest door.

chapters.title: The Ledger of Sainte-Marthe
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. In the church archive she finds the winter ledger: every generation, one household 'counted in' and struck from all records—photos, memories, gravestones. Her borrowed name is already inked in this winter's column. Beat: horror of being pre-claimed.

chapters.title: Bram Speaks
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Bram finally speaks: he survived a counted-in household as a boy by hiding in the bell tower the night the bell still hung. He explains the count needs every member present. Beat: found family forged in shared terror.

chapters.title: Running Water, Running Roads
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. She tries to flee with the family; the road loops back to Sainte-Marthe no matter which way they drive. The radio plays their own voices, pre-recorded, saying things they never said. Beat: claustrophobia, the trap of the village.

chapters.title: The Curator of Names
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. She seeks the oldest resident, blind Père Anselme, who explains the covenant: the village erased the dead to survive, and the dead want only their names back. He warns the count cannot be cheated—only answered. Beat: the rules of the horror clarified.

chapters.title: Théo's Bargain
chapters.summary: Théo's POV. Théo secretly calls his mother back and agrees to be counted in exchange for the family's release. The line goes warm. He packs a bag. Beat: heartbreak—the price of survival offered by the youngest.

chapters.title: Missing
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Théo is gone at dawn; the ledger now lists him under the Joubert household. Elodie realizes her false name drew the count to her family. Beat: guilt detonating into resolve.

chapters.title: The Tower at Dusk
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Bram and Elodie climb the empty bell tower as the bell rings from nowhere; Bram nearly walks off the edge, called by his old household's voices. Elodie drags him back by his coat. Beat: the dead's pull made physical.

chapters.title: Interference
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. On air, the dead begin speaking through her broadcast, over her voice. She fights for the microphone and realizes the signal runs both ways: they can reach out, but so can she. Beat: turn from victim to adversary.

chapters.title: What the Village Forgot
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. She digs into parish registers: the 1911 bell was cast with the names of plague dead engraved inside—names the village melted rather than remember. The covenant began that winter. Beat: the mystery's engine revealed.

chapters.title: The Count
chapters.summary: Multiple brief POVs. Dusk; the bell rings continuously; doors open on their own; villagers walk the streets answering roll call of their erased kin. Madame Roux confesses her household was meant to be offered this year—until Elodie's name appeared. Beat: the village's complicity exposed.

chapters.title: Théo, Found
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. She finds Théo at the churchyard, standing before his mother's unmarked grave, half-gone, voice already thin. She refuses to let him go and instead says his mother's full name aloud—and the pull on him falters. Beat: the first proof remembering works.

chapters.title: Broadcast the Dead
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Climax begins: she locks herself in the studio and reads every erased name from the ledger on air, hour after hour, while the dead crowd the frequency and the bell tolls faster. Beat: defiance as ritual.

chapters.title: The Bell Answers
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Climax. With the last name spoken, the bell rings once, loudly, inside the tower that holds no bell—and cracks the air like glass. The dead speak not as claimants but as witnesses; the count collapses, its arithmetic broken by remembrance. Beat: terror transfigured into release.

chapters.title: After the Tolling
chapters.summary: Théo's POV. Morning. The village remembers a little—Roux weeps at a grave that now bears a name. Théo is fully back but changed, carrying his mother's voice like a coal. Beat: grief and gratitude braided.

chapters.title: A House for the Winter
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. The family prepares to leave, but Elodie knows a covenant broken must be tended, not abandoned. She sends Théo and Bram ahead with the car and stays one winter as the village's night voice, reading names so the count never reforms. Beat: sacrifice reframed as vocation.

chapters.title: Sign-Off
chapters.summary: Bram's POV, closing. Spring: Bram and Théo return for her, and find Elodie at the microphone, translucent at the edges but smiling, doing the show that keeps the dead at peace. She signs off with her true name for the first time. Beat: bittersweet resolution—found family persists across the threshold.
